activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A new baby will often hold tight to a finger placed in its hand.
story:
Henri ran up the steps to Grandma's house. Today he would meet the new baby. Grandma opened the door fast. "She is here," Grandma said. "She is so small."

Henri tiptoed to the basket. The baby was tiny. She had little hands. She was sleeping. Henri wanted her to wake up. He wanted her to look at him.

"Can I touch her hand?" Henri asked. Grandma nodded. Henri put one finger near the baby. The baby's hand opened. Then it closed. She held his finger tight! Henri laughed. He pulled his arm a little. The baby still held on. "Grandma, look!" Henri said. "She likes me!" The baby opened her eyes. She looked right at Henri. Grandma smiled and got the camera. "Say worm," said Grandma, because the baby was small and pink. But Henri stood frozen, so happy. The baby kept his finger. She would not let go. "I will follow you everywhere," Henri told her. Then the baby let out a big yawn. At last she let go. Henri waved. "Bye, little hand," he said.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A square has four sides that are all the same length.
story:
Mateo sat at the art table. He had a big purple crayon. He wanted to draw a house with a window.

"First I need a square," said Mateo. He drew four lines. But one line was too short. The square looked crooked. "Oh no," said Mateo.

His teacher gave him a cracker. "Look," she said. "This cracker is a square." Mateo was not sure. He took a piece of string from the craft box. He laid the string on one side. Then he laid it on the next side. Then the next one. Then the last one. All four sides took the same string! The cracker was a square.

Mateo smiled. He drew four lines again. He made each line the same length. Now he had a real square. He drew a triangle on top for the roof. He drew a little round circle for the doorknob. Then he drew a baby sleeping inside, and a rectangle for the door.

"I did it!" said Mateo. His teacher poured him a tiny cup of juice. Mateo munched his square cracker, crunch, crunch, crunch.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: In a pretend shop, one person can be the shopkeeper and another can be the shopper.
story:
Paisley wanted to play shop at school. Ben had set out little pots on a table. "Welcome to my shop," said Ben. "I am the shopkeeper."

Paisley picked up a tiny red pot. "I want this one," she said. She gave Ben a bottle cap for money. "Thank you, shopper," said Ben. He put the cap in his shoe.

Then Ben wanted to buy too. He waited behind a block wall like a shopper on a road to town. Paisley sat in the shopkeeper chair. She held up a tiny sock. "This sock is not stinky," she said. "It smells like flowers." Ben laughed and paid two caps.

After shop time, they dug in the sand tray outside. Paisley buried the red pot and dug it up again. "Let's play shop tomorrow," said Ben. "Yes," said Paisley. "I will be the shopkeeper next."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a cloudy day, clouds can hide the sun.
story:
Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. It was a sunny morning. The sun made his toes feel warm in his sandals. Then a big cloud came. The sun went away. "Where did the sun go?" Harrison asked. "The cloud is hiding it," said Mama. Harrison looked up. He could not see the sun at all.

Then the wind began to blow. It blew Mama's scarf. It ruffled Harrison's hair. The cloud turned gray. Rain fell down, tap tap tap. "Brr," said Harrison. His toes were cold now. Mama opened a little umbrella. They stood under it together. The rain made dots on the ground.

They waited and waited. Harrison watched the sky. The gray cloud moved away, slow and soft. The sun came out again. "Hello, sun!" said Harrison. His toes got warm once more. Mama put the umbrella down. The wet road turned shiny and sweet in the sun.

The bus came round the corner. Harrison held Mama's hand. They climbed up the steps together. "I saw the cloud hide the sun," said Harrison. Mama smiled at him. The bus door closed with a soft little whoosh.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut to remember it.
story:
Henri sat in the big waiting chair. He hugged his doll tight. Today he would get his very first haircut. He did not want the scissors to come near his doll.

"Mama will hold her," said Mama. She set the doll on her lap. Henri climbed up into the salon chair all by himself. The lady picked up her scissors. Snip, snip went a little curl. The curl fell down. It landed on the cape like a soft brown ring.

Mama picked up the curl. She put it in a small envelope. "Why?" asked Henri. "To keep," said Mama. She tucked the envelope in her bag. Henri looked in the mirror. His hair was short now, and the curl was safe too. He gave the mirror a big silly grin. "Home now," he said. Mama laughed and took his hand.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: When a birthday cake has candles, a grown-up is the one who lights them.
story:
Leah turned three today. The party was in the backyard. A big cake sat on the picnic table. Mom had put three candles on top. Leah held a little match in her hand.

Dad knelt down near her. He took the match gently. "I light the candles," he said. "You can help after." Dad touched the match to each candle. One, two, three little flames. Leah hopped up and down on one foot. The flames made little warm lights on the cake.

Everyone came close to the table. "Now you," Dad said. Leah took a big breath. She blew and blew. The flames went out. Smoke curled up like a soft gray ribbon. Grandma clapped. The friends clapped too. Leah looked at the candles. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. Dad laughed and cut the cake.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: In and out are opposites.
story:
Beatrice went to the store with Dad. She wanted a big red ball. On the shelf were big balls and small balls. Beatrice picked a big one. It was too big for her hands. So she picked a small one instead. "This one fits," she said.

Near the bread, the oven door was open. Dad said, "That oven is hot. Stay back." Beatrice stayed back. Then she touched the cold milk box. "Brrr," she said. "Cold!" Dad smiled.

At the toy bin, a baby kept taking toys out. Beatrice put a toy in. The baby took it out. Beatrice put it in again. Out it came again. The baby giggled. "You like out," said Beatrice. "I like in. In and out are not the same!" She put a toy in fast. The baby pulled it out slow. Dad laughed. "What a silly game," he said. "Can I play too?" Beatrice handed him a toy. "Put it in, Dad," she said.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We feel things by touching them with our skin, like our fingertips.
story:
Sofia wanted to be a big kid. Big kids know five whole senses. Sofia knew only one. That felt like a problem.

Mama had an idea. She put a soft sock over Sofia's eyes. "Now we play a guessing game," said Mama. She put things in Sofia's hands, one at a time.

Sofia held a cold spoon. She held a fuzzy peach. She held a bumpy rock. She did not peek. She used her fingertips. The fingertips told her things. "The peach is soft!" said Sofia. "The rock is bumpy!" Her fingertips felt it all. Sofia smiled big. Touching was a sense too.

Then Mama held up her hand. "Can you turn around fast?" she asked. Sofia spun around. The sock slipped off. On the table was a cookie, warm from the oven. Sofia could smell it with her nose. She could see it with her eyes. "Three senses!" said Sofia. "I can hear you munch." Mama laughed.

Soon it would be the moon's turn to come up. Sofia ate her cookie slowly. "Tomorrow I will learn the last one," she said. Mama kissed her head. "That one is easy," said Mama. "You will love it." Sofia held Mama's hand. Her fingertips felt warm.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a snowy day, mittens or gloves keep your hands warm.
story:
Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he shouted. Big white snow was falling down. It fell on the slide. It fell on the swings.

Miss Ana held up a sign. It had a snowflake on it. "Snowy day!" she said. "Time for snow pants and boots!"

Grayson zipped his puffy coat. He pulled his hat on. Everyone ran outside. The snow crunched under his boots. It was cold and soft.

"I will make the biggest snowball!" said Grayson. He scooped and patted. His ball grew big and round.

His friend Milo made a snowball too. But Milo's hands turned red. "Ow, ow," said Milo. He had no mittens. His hands were cold. Grayson had fuzzy blue mittens. His hands stayed warm inside them.

"Here," said Grayson. He shared one mitten with Milo. Milo put it on one hand. Then Miss Ana found a spare pair in the big basket.

"Miss Ana!" yelled Milo. "My hands feel warm now!" He held up his mittened hands like they won a prize.

Grayson smiled a shy smile. Then he pushed his big snowball down the hill. It rolled and rolled and got even bigger. "Come on!" he called. "Let's build a snow man!"

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: People say 'thank you' after someone gives them something or helps them.
story:
Wren sat at the dinner table. She wore her big red hat. Dad said the hat would not work at the table. It fell into the soup. So she took it off.

Wren wanted more potatoes. She reached far across the table. Her cup tipped over. Milk went everywhere. Wren felt her face go hot. "Sorry," she said softly. "That is okay," said Dad. He wiped the milk with a cloth. Mom brought a towel too. "Can you help me?" Wren asked. Mom helped her wipe her chair.

Then Wren tried again. "More potatoes, please," she said. Dad smiled and gave her some. Wren ate a bite. They were warm and good. She was not a lazy eater tonight. She looked up at Dad. "Thank you," she said. Dad passed her the bread too. "Thank you," Wren said again, and took a big bite.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: When you find something that belongs to someone else, you give it back to them.
story:
Livia lost her bunny. Bunny was soft and pink. Livia looked under her bed. No bunny there.

She peeked in the toy box. She saw a small red car. The car was not hers. The car was her brother Sam's car. Sam had looked for it yesterday. "When you find something that belongs to someone else, you give it back to them." Livia ran to Sam. "I found your car!" she said. Sam smiled big. "Thank you, Livia!"

Sam wanted to help her too. They looked in the hall. They looked by the big chair. No bunny. "Maybe bunny is far away," said Sam. They peeked behind the couch. It was dark back there. Livia reached in her hand.

Something soft touched her fingers. She pulled it out. It was bunny! Livia hugged bunny tight. Sam clapped his hands. "Yay!" he said. Livia put the red car in Sam's hand. Sam put bunny in Livia's arms.

Then they sat together on the rug. Sam pushed the car. "Vroom," he said. Livia made bunny hop. "Hop, hop, bunny," she said.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A grandparent is a parent of your mom or your dad.
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Sienna held her hand at the market. The stalls smelled like bread and peaches.

"Can we buy apples?" Sienna asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "Your mom loved apples when she was little."

Sienna stopped walking. "You know my mom when she was little?"

Grandma smiled. "I am her mom too."

Sienna looked up. "You are a mom? But you are a grandma!"

"Both," said Grandma.

Sienna thought hard. So Grandma was Mom's mom. Just like Mom was her mom. She squeezed Grandma's hand.

Then Sienna saw a paint stand. Bright paints in little jars. Red, blue, and yellow.

"Can we paint together?" she asked.

"We can paint a clock for your room," said Grandma.

At home, Mom helped set out the paper. Sienna painted a big round face. Grandma painted the numbers. Mom painted the hands.

The paint dried by the window. It took a long time, but Sienna waited.

At bedtime, the clock hung far above her bed. Mom, Grandma, and Sienna stood back to look.

"We all made it," said Sienna.

Grandma kissed the top of her head. "Moms and grandmas and girls," she said. "That is how it goes."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread.
story:
Emilia sat at the big table. Mom put warm toast on her plate. "I want to do it myself," Emilia said. Mom gave her a small knife with a round edge. Mom held the butter dish close.

Emilia poked the toast with the pointy tip of the knife. The toast got a hole in it. Butter fell off in little lumps. An ant crawled near the plate, looking for crumbs. "Hmm," said Emilia.

Mom turned the knife over. The flat side shined in the light. Emilia took some butter on the flat side. She pushed it across the bread, slow and slow. The butter went smooth all over. No holes. No lumps. Just smooth, shiny toast.

Next came the milk. Emilia held the little cup with both hands. She poured, drip by drip. One small drop ran down the side. She wiped it with her finger. She tried again. This time nothing spilled at all.

Emilia bit her toast. "I did it," she said. Mom sat down beside her and poured her own milk.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Putting a toy back in the same place each time makes it easy to find.
story: Anthony rode the bus with his mama. He held his little blue bunny. The bus went bump, bump, bump. Bunny jumped out of his hands! Anthony looked down. Where did bunny go? He peeked under the seat. He saw a shoe. He saw a gum wrapper. No bunny. Then mama lifted the seat flap. There was bunny! The bus went bump, and bunny had slid under. Anthony hugged bunny tight. "Was bunny hiding?" he asked. At home, Anthony found a clean box. He put a soft sock inside. "This is bunny's nest," he said. Every night, bunny slept in the same nest by his bed. One morning Anthony could not see bunny. He looked at the nest. There sat bunny, waiting. "It's true," said Anthony. "The nest keeps bunny easy to find." He smiled and gave bunny a kiss.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: Front teeth are for biting food, and back teeth are for chewing it.
story:
Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist. It was her first time.

"I want to be brave," said Florence.

"We can go slow," said Mama.

At the dentist, a kind lady looked in Florence's mouth. "Open big," she said. Florence opened. The lady counted her teeth. "All done," she said. Florence got a sticker shaped like a fish. It was blue and shiny.

On the bus home, a boy sat near them. His mama gave him an apple slice. The boy bit it with his front teeth. Then he moved it to his back teeth and chomped. The apple got small. Then it was gone.

Florence watched. She had a biscuit in her bag. She took it out. She bit it with her front teeth. The biscuit made a crunch. Then she moved it to her back teeth. She chomped and chomped. The biscuit got small. It tasted sweet.

"Look, Mama," said Florence. "Front bites, back chomps."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown.
story:
Leah ran to the big slide at the playground. She wanted to be a rocket ship today. Her friend Sam was already at the top. "I am a rocket," he said. "But I need help. I forgot how rockets start."

Leah thought hard. She had heard counting at home. Mommy counted apples at the store, one, two, three. At school they sang a number song, all the way to ten. But rockets did not go up that way.

"I know," Leah said. "We count the other way. Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one." Sam held the line of the slide with both hands. "Then what?" he asked. "Then blast off!" Leah said.

Sam counted with her. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Sam zoomed down the slide and jumped up at the end. He was so happy. "You did it!" he said.

A small boy stood by the ladder. He looked sad. "I want a rocket too," he said. "I don't know the numbers." Leah took his hand. "Come with me," she said. "We will count together."

They stood in a line at the ladder. Leah helped the little boy climb up. Then he called out, "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Down he came, fast and laughing. Leah clapped and said, "One more rocket is ready."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot.
story:
Arthur dug in Grandpa's garden. He planted little seeds with his hands. Grandpa helped him pat the soil. "Where did we put the tomatoes?" Arthur asked. He could not remember. He looked at the dirt. All the rows looked the same. Arthur scratched his head.

Then Grandpa held up a stick. A paper picture was on it. It showed a red tomato. Grandpa pushed the stick into the soil. "Now this spot has a name," he said. Arthur clapped his hands. He ran inside for more paper. He drew a long orange carrot. He drew a round yellow squash. He put a stick in the middle of every row.

Day by day, green shoots popped up. Arthur froze when he saw a tiny sprout. "Which one is it?" he gasped. He ran to look at the labels. The sprout was by the carrot picture. "Carrots! Carrots are growing!" he shouted. Grandpa laughed. Arthur counted the labels. "One, two, three rows!" Every row knew its own name. Arthur watered them all and said, "Grow big, little labels!"

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A week has seven days.
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Juliette's house. He wore a big blue hat. Juliette gave him a hug. Then Mommy took them to the market.

At the market, Juliette saw apples. She saw bread. She saw a dog with a waggy tail. Grandpa said, "I can stay for a week." Juliette did not know how long a week was. She asked, "When do you go home?" Grandpa said, "We will count the days."

At home, Mommy showed Juliette the calendar. Juliette drew a red circle on one day. That was day one. The next morning, she drew another circle. Day two! Each morning, she drew one more circle. Day three, day four, day five, day six.

Juliette counted her circles. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Only six circles. She was sorry. She thought the week was over. "Is today your last day?" she asked. Grandpa said, "Count again with me." Juliette pointed at each circle. Then she drew one more. Seven circles!

"A week has seven days!" said Juliette. Grandpa laughed and clapped. On the seventh day, he put on his big blue hat. Juliette waved and waved at the door. "Come back for seven more circles!" she called. Grandpa waved his hat in the air.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help.
story:
Owen ran to the park with his dad. He felt so excited. The slide was tall and red.

Near the slide, a girl was crying. She looked sad. Her kite was stuck in a tree. "I want my kite," she said.

Then a big dog ran by. It barked very loud. Owen felt scared. He ran to his dad. "Dad, the dog scared me," he said. His dad held his hand. "I will help you," said Dad. They walked to the bench together. Owen watched the dog from far away. The dog was only playing with a smelly old ball. Owen began to feel a little better.

His dad asked the dog's owner for help. The tall man got the kite down from the tree. The girl smiled big. Now she looked happy. She ran with her kite, and it flew up high.

Owen clapped. He felt happy too. "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. His dad laughed. "Yes," he said. "And if you ever feel scared, just tell me." Owen nodded. He took one more ride down the big red slide.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: After you sleep tonight and wake up, today will be called yesterday.
story:
Penelope wanted to paint a cat at school. Yesterday she had painted a dog. Today she wanted a cat with a long tail. But the paint shelf was empty. "No more orange," said her teacher. "Come back tomorrow."

Penelope frowned. "Where did today go?" she asked her dad at bedtime. He tucked her in. "After you sleep tonight and wake up, today will be called yesterday," he said. Penelope closed her eyes.

She slept. The sun came in low through the window. She woke up and put on her shoes. "Yesterday is done," she said. At school, she walked to the paint shelf. New orange paint sat on the top. Penelope painted her cat with a long tail. "Now it is today," she said, and held it up. "A cat!"

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: A book's title is its name.
story:
Jasmine wanted her book about the rainbow. She looked at her shelf. So many books! She pulled one out. She looked at the front cover. The words said "Sleepy Bunny". That was not it.

Jasmine asked, "Where is my rainbow book?"
Mama said, "Look for its name."
"But books don't talk," said Jasmine.
"The name is written there," said Mama. She pointed to the big words at the top.

Jasmine put "Sleepy Bunny" back on the shelf. She pulled out another book. She looked at the big words. They said "Rainbow Moon". She held it up. "This one!" she said.

"That's the one," said Mama.

Jasmine opened the front cover. Page one came first. Mama read it to her. Jasmine turned each page, one by one, all the way to the end. The last page had a big orange moon.

"Again," said Jasmine.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange.
story:
Henry sat at the paint table. He wanted to paint a big pumpkin. But there was no orange paint.

He looked and looked. He saw red paint. He saw yellow paint. "One, two, no orange," said Henry.

His teacher Miss Jo sat down next to him. "What do you need, Henry?" she asked.

"I need orange for my pumpkin," said Henry.

Miss Jo gave him a white paper cup. Henry put in some red paint. Drip, drip. He put in some yellow paint. Drip, drip. He mixed it round and round with his brush.

The paint turned orange!

Henry stared at the cup. He dipped his brush. He painted the big pumpkin. Red and yellow made orange, all by mixing.

His friend Milo came over. Milo had a sad face. "I want orange too," said Milo.

Henry gave Milo his white cup. "Here," he said. "You can mix with me."

They painted together. Milo tickled the paper with his brush. One pumpkin, two pumpkins, three pumpkins.

"Happy Halloween!" said Henry, and he held up his orange pumpkin for everyone to see.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: When a friend shares with you, saying 'thank you' shows you noticed their kindness.
story:
Max saw the big red truck at school. Ben had it first. Max wanted it so much. He reached out his hand to grab it. Then he stopped. He put his hands in his pockets instead.

"Can I have a turn?" Max asked. Ben looked at him. "You can have it after this," said Ben. Max sat on the pillow to wait. His sweater was itchy, so he tugged his sleeve while he waited. It was hard to wait. He watched Ben push the truck up the ramp.

Then Ben held out the truck. "Your turn," said Ben. Max took it with both hands. "Thank you," he said. Ben smiled a big smile. Then Ben sat on the pillow to wait, just like Max did.

Max pushed the truck fast. It rolled under the table. A little kitten was hiding there! The kitten batted the truck with one paw. Ben laughed and laughed. Max got down on his knees to look. "Truck for the kitty too," said Max.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: A person's name is written with a capital letter at the start.
story:
Riley sat at the little blue table. She had a crayon in her hand. Miss Ana gave her a paper with letters on it.

"Find the R," said Miss Ana. Riley looked. She looked some more. She pointed at a small r. "That one!" she said. "Yes," said Miss Ana. "That is r. It says rrr." Riley made the sound too. "Rrr," she said, and laughed.

Then Miss Ana wrote Riley's name. "Riley starts with R," she said. Riley took the crayon. She wrote her name all by herself. But her first letter was small. She looked at Miss Ana's writing. That first letter was big. It stood tall.

Riley tapped her small r with her finger. She looked again. Then she drew a big R on top. The big R stood up tall, just like the big girl letter in Miss Ana's writing. "Look!" said Riley. She held up the paper. "My name! Big R!"

"Good work," said Miss Ana. "Time to go wash hands for dinner." Riley carried her paper with her, holding it high.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed.
story:
David waited by the gate at school. He saw his grandma come walking up. She had his green hat in her bag.

"Time to go home," said Grandma. "You can help me today."

At home, David ate his snack. He ate apple slices that Grandma cut into small pieces. Then he had a nap on his little bed.

When he woke up, Grandma said, "Bath time." David took off his socks and his shirt. He left them on the floor.

Then he looked at the laundry basket. He picked up a sock. He threw it. It went in the basket. He picked up the other sock. It went in too. "Basket!" said David. He threw his shirt. It landed on the edge. He pushed it in with his hand.

After his bath, David put on soft pajamas. The dirty clothes stayed in the basket. "They will get washed," said Grandma.

David pointed at the basket. "More socks tomorrow," he said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Later means some time after now, not right away.
story:
Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the big strawberry on her plate. "Can I eat the strawberry now?" she asked. Mom said, "Eat your peas first. You can have the strawberry later." Sadie looked at the strawberry. It was red, her favorite color. "Is it later yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. Sadie ate one pea. "Is it later yet?" "Not yet." Sadie ate another pea, and another. "Is it later yet?" Mom smiled. "Now it is later." Sadie was happy. She picked up the strawberry and took a big bite.

Then Dad said, "Yesterday we had bananas. Today we have strawberries. Tomorrow we will have apples." Sadie counted on her fingers. Yesterday, today, tomorrow. "Can we talk about tomorrow now?" she asked. Dad laughed. "We can talk about it now, and eat it later." Sadie looked at her plate. Later was after now. She had made later come, all by eating her peas. She held up the last strawberry piece. "This is now!" she said.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Some letters are made of straight lines, like L, and some have curves, like O.
story:
Charlie ran to the writing table. Today he would write his name! Miss Amy gave him a fat pencil. "Grip it like this," she said. Charlie held it tight. He pushed the pencil down the road of paper. The letters came out wobbly.

"C, H, A..." Charlie stopped. The C looked like a squiggle. "Yucky C!" he said. He looked at Ben's name. Ben was sorting letter cards. "Look," said Ben. "L is all straight lines. O is all curves." Charlie picked up his card. L had straight sticks. O was round like a ball.

Charlie tried again. He drew two straight sticks for his H. One, two! Then he made a big round curve for his C. It looked good! "I did it!" he shouted. He lifted his paper up high. "C for Charlie! C with a curve!" Miss Amy clapped. Charlie grinned and wrote his whole name, one letter at a time.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
story:
Jayden sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin on his paper plate. But he had no orange paint. His jars held red, blue, yellow and green. "No orange," said Jayden. "That is bad."

Grandma set the jars in a row. "One red, two blue, three yellow, four green," she said. Jayden dipped his brush in the red. He made a red dot on his plate. Then he dipped in the yellow. He stirred the two dots together. The paint turned orange! "Look, Grandma!" said Jayden. "Red and yellow make orange!"

He painted his pumpkin round and bright. Then he added a green leaf and a blue sky. "My pumpkin looks real," said Jayden. Grandma held it up to the sunny window. "One pumpkin, one leaf, one happy boy," she said, and hung it on the wall.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A pair means two, like a pair of socks.
story:
Amira wanted to wear her new socks. She opened her sock drawer. She pulled out one red sock. Then she looked and looked. Where was the other sock?

"One sock," said Amira. "I need two." She put the sock on her foot. Her other foot was still bare. She counted her toes. "One, two, three, four, five. Toes need socks too."

Amira searched the laundry basket. She counted the socks she found. "One, two, three." None of them were red. She looked under her bed. Dust made her nose scratch. No red sock there.

Then she saw something behind the door. It was small and red. It was the other sock! "A pair!" said Amira. She put it on her bare foot. Now both feet were warm.

Amira ran to show Mama. "Mama, look! Two socks!" Mama smiled. She held up her own feet. She was wearing one blue sock and one yellow sock. "Oh no," said Mama. "Now I need a match."

"I will help you," said Amira. She took Mama's hand. Together they went to the sock drawer. "Let's count them all," said Amira. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten socks in a big pile, waiting to make pairs.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy.
story:
Aurora sat down at the dinner table. She saw a big bowl in the middle. Steam rose up from it. "What is that?" she asked. "Soup," said Mama. "You will see."

Aurora sniffed with her nose. Mmm, it smelled like carrots. Then she heard a funny sound. Pop, pop, went the bread in the toaster. Her ears heard it first!

Mama put three little things by Aurora's plate. "Close your eyes," said Mama. "Now touch." Aurora felt one thing. It was soft. "Feather!" she said. She felt the next one. It was rough and bumpy. "Pinecone!" She felt the last one. It was smooth and cool. "My stone!" She opened her eyes. She was right, right, right.

Aurora took a small sip of soup. Her tongue tasted carrots. "More bread, please," she said. The toaster popped again. Aurora laughed. "The bread jumps when it is hot!" She painted a picture of the jumping bread with her carrot on her plate, and the bowl of soup sat grumpy and steamy in the middle, waiting.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Standing closer to the hoop makes it easier to get the beanbag in.
story:
Camille put on her warm mittens. Today was hockey rink day! The ice was far away, and the smooth floor by the rink was for games. Camille saw a red hoop on the floor and a small beanbag in her hand.

"Can I get it in?" she asked her dad.

"You can try," he said.

Camille threw the beanbag. It fell far from the hoop. She threw again. It missed again. Camille frowned. Then she took three little steps closer to the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It went in! The beanbag sank right down in the middle of the hoop.

"I did it!" she shouted. Dad clapped his hands. Camille jumped up and down.

Next came the big blue ball. Dad rolled it to her. Camille held out both hands. The ball bumped her tummy and fell. Dad rolled it again, slow and easy. Camille opened her arms wide. The ball came right into her hands.

"I caught it! Can I throw the beanbag one more time?"

"Yes, one more big throw," said Dad.

Camille stood close to the hoop. She threw the beanbag high. It sank in again.

"That was pretty great," said Dad. He wrapped Camille in her soft blanket. "Time for warm cocoa."

Camille hugged the ball all the way home.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: A cup with nothing in it is empty, and a cup filled to the top is full.
story: Jasmine wanted to fill her cup at the little sink in the playroom. The cup was empty. It had nothing inside. She turned the tap fast. Water splashed out fast and sploshed over the top. "Oh no," said Jasmine. She mopped it up with a towel. She tried again. This time she made the water go slow. Slow, slow, drip. The cup began to fill. It got full to the top. Then she turned the tap off. Not one drop spilled. "I did it!" she said. Daddy clapped from the big chair. Then he brought her a small cup of cocoa. It was hot, so Daddy held it. Jasmine waited and waited. Then she took a tiny lick. It was warm and sweet, not sour like the lemon she once tried. Her toy duck on a string sat beside her. It was small, and the water cup was big. Jasmine smiled and drank it all, slow sip by slow sip.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day.
story:
Quinn went to the pet store with Dad. She saw fish and birds and one small kitten. The kitten was in a box with soft blankets. "This one," said Quinn. "She is coming home with us," said Dad.

At home, the kitten drank and drank. Then she played. Then she slept. In the morning, Quinn ran to see her. The water bowl was empty! The kitten sat by it and looked sad. "She wants more water," said Quinn.

Quinn tried to reach the sink, but it was too high. "I will help," said Dad. Dad turned on the tap. Quinn held the bowl under the cool water. It filled up, splash by splash. "Fresh water for you," said Quinn.

She set the bowl down by the kitten's food. The kitten ran over right away. She lapped and lapped until the bowl was half empty. Quinn patted her soft head. The kitten purred. "Every day I will fill your bowl," said Quinn. The kitten blinked at her, then curled up to sleep.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: One thing can belong to more than one group, like an apple is a food and also a fruit.
story:
Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels. "I want my apple," said Felix. Mama reached into the bag. She gave him a red apple. It felt cool and smooth in his hands.

Then Felix saw his picture cards on the seat. One card showed fruits. Bananas, grapes, and oranges. One card showed foods. Bread, cheese, and milk. Felix held up his apple to the fruit card. "Apple goes here," he said. Then he held it by the food card. "No, apple goes here." He looked and looked. His sister Maya leaned over. "Apple is a fruit," she said. "Apple is a food," said Felix.

Mama smiled in the mirror. "Let's see," she said. Felix put the apple on the fruit card. Then he put it on the food card too. It sat on both cards at once. "Two spots!" said Felix. Maya clapped. Bump, bump went the wheels. Felix took one big bite. Crunch! "My apple is a food and a fruit," he said. Maya laughed and gave him a napkin. "Surprise!" said Felix, juice dripping down his chin. "One apple, two cards." The car drove on and on.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: In hide-and-seek, the seeker counts while the others hide.
story: Alice went to the playground with her friends. "Let's play hide-and-seek," said Ben. "You seek, Alice. Close your eyes and count to ten." Alice closed her eyes. She counted very fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She turned around. Nobody was hiding yet. Mia stood in the open. Ben ran to the slide too late. "Alice, count slowly," said Mia. "Then we can hide." "Why slowly?" asked Alice. "Because we need time to hide," said Mia. Alice nodded. She closed her eyes again. This time she counted slowly. "One, two, three, four..." Mia hid behind the bush. "Five, six, seven..." Ben climbed under the bridge, careful not to bump his head. "Eight, nine, ten." Alice opened her eyes. The playground was quiet. Where did they go? She looked by the swing. She looked at the sandbox. Then she saw Mia's shoe stick out by the bush. "I see you, Mia!" Mia laughed and came out. They looked for Ben together. Alice found a slimy snail on a leaf. She did not touch it. She just looked. Then she heard a giggle. Ben was under the bridge! "Found you," said Alice. "That was fun," said Ben. "Let's play again. I had a dream about this game last night, and we all won." They all held hands and skipped to the swings.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'no, thank you' is a polite way to say you don't want something.
story:
Hayden went to the library with his mom. The sky was cloudy, so it was a good day to stay inside. He wanted one special book, a book with a cat on the cover.

At the story table, a girl named Mia had cookies. She held the box out to Hayden. "Want one?" she asked. Hayden looked at the cookie. It had raisins in it. He did not like raisins. "Yuck!" he said loudly. The library lady put her finger to her lips. "Shh," she said softly. Hayden felt his face get warm.

Mom knelt down next to him. "Try again," she whispered. Mia held out the box one more time. Hayden took a big breath. "No, thank you," he said. Mia smiled. "Okay!" she said. Then she found a plain cookie in her bag and gave it to him. "This one has no raisins," she said. "Thank you," said Hayden. He munched his cookie while the library lady found the cat book, hiding behind three big books. It was the last one on the shelf, and it was his.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Only a grown-up gives a child medicine.
story:
Brooks was getting over his cold. His nose still ran a little. His cough came at night. So Mama took him to the pharmacy.

The pharmacy had bright lights. There were big shelves full of boxes. A lady in a white coat waved at Brooks. He waved back from Mama's side.

Mama picked out a small bottle. She put it on the counter. The bottle had a purple cap. Brooks looked at it. He wanted to open it himself. He reached up his hand.

Mama shook her head. She held the bottle high. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," she said. She showed him the little cup. It had lines on it. Mama poured the medicine slowly. The liquid went up to one line. Then she stopped.

At home, Mama sat by Brooks. She gave him the little cup. He drank it all down. It tasted like grapes.

The last thing before bed, Brooks looked at the bottle on the high shelf. He pointed at it and said, "That's Mama's job." Mama smiled and turned off the light.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Milk goes back in the fridge after pouring, to keep it cold.
story:
Louis stood at the little table. Toast sat on his plate. So did a cup of milk.

"Watch me," said Miss Ana. She took her knife. She spread butter on her toast. The butter slid from edge to edge. Louis picked up his own knife. He spread slowly. The butter made soft waves. "I did it!" said Louis. Then he lifted the milk jug with both hands. He poured a little bit. Then a little bit more. Not one drop fell. His heart felt big and happy.

Miss Ana clapped. Louis drank some milk. Then he ran off to play. The milk stayed on the table. He saw it sitting there. "Oh no! You go back in the fridge," he said. He carried the milk to Miss Ana. She opened the fridge door. Louis set the milk inside, where it was far from the warm room. "Good job, Louis," said Miss Ana. Louis smiled and went to chase his friend Sam across the room.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Heavy and light are opposites.
story:
Connor wanted to build a big tower in his playroom. He saw a heavy box of blocks under the shelf. He pulled it. It did not move. He pulled again. Still no move!

"Why is this so hard?" he asked.

His teddy sat on top of a light feather pillow. Connor picked up the pillow with one hand. Up it went, so easy! He wondered, "Can the pillow help me?" He put the dirty pillow on the floor and sat on it. Then he pushed the box with his feet, slow and steady. The box slid a little. He pushed fast. It slid more!

Mama heard him and came in. "Let's carry the blocks together," she said. "You take the light bag. I'll take the heavy box."

Connor filled his small red bag. It was light in his hands. Soon he had a big, tall tower. He put the teddy on top, soft and slow. "Hello up there!" said Connor.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: A grown-up should check that bath water is warm, not hot, before you get in.
story:
Asher ran to the park with his mom. He wanted to go down the big slide. He touched the slide with one finger. The slide was hot. The sun had made it hot. Asher pulled his hand back fast.

"Too hot," said Mom. She put her hand on it too. "Let's find the shady slide." They found a small slide under a tree. Asher touched it. This slide was cool. He went down, down, down. "Again!" he said. Mom laughed. Asher was happy. He drank his juice in the shade. Then it was time to bring his trucks home and get ready for bath.

At home, the tub filled with water. Asher wanted to jump right in. He remembered the hot slide. He stopped his feet. "Mom, check it first," he said. Mom put her hand in the water. "It is warm, not hot," she said. Asher put in one toe. The water felt nice. His little toy duck was already floating there. "Quack!" said Asher, and he climbed in slow.
